summary: harborbakery.example scored 61/100 (grade D) on 20 passive checks. 9 items need attention. Start with: Directory listing.

findings.evidence: https://harborbakery.example/ answered over an encrypted connection.
findings.title: HTTPS works
findings.what: Your site loads over an encrypted HTTPS connection, so what visitors type and see can't be read in transit.

findings.evidence: Trusted certificate for harborbakery.example, www.harborbakery.example, issued by Let's Encrypt.
findings.title: Certificate is trusted
findings.what: Your SSL certificate is valid and trusted by browsers.

findings.evidence: Certificate valid until Nov 14, 2026 (40 days from now).
findings.title: Certificate expiry
findings.what: Your certificate isn't close to expiring.

findings.evidence: Connected with TLSv1.3.
findings.title: Modern TLS version
findings.what: The secure connection uses a modern version of TLS (the encryption behind HTTPS).

findings.evidence: Outdated TLS 1.0 and 1.1 connections are refused.
findings.title: Old TLS 1.0/1.1 turned off
findings.what: The server refuses the old, weak TLS 1.0 and 1.1 versions.

findings.evidence: http:// redirects to HTTPS: http://harborbakery.example (301) → https://harborbakery.example (200)
findings.title: HTTP redirects to HTTPS
findings.what: Visitors who type or click an http:// link are sent to the secure version.

findings.evidence: Found insecure images/media: http://harborbakery.example/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/cakes.jpg (home page only).
findings.title: No insecure (mixed) content
findings.what: Your home page loads some images or media over insecure http:// links. Browsers may block them or show a warning.
findings.fix: Change those http:// links to https:// (or to relative links) in your site's pages or theme.

findings.evidence: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=300 (5 minutes; 180+ days is recommended)
findings.title: HSTS (Strict-Transport-Security)
findings.what: HSTS is set, but for a short time, so browsers forget it quickly.
findings.fix: Raise the max-age to at least 15552000 (180 days); one year (31536000) is common.

findings.evidence: No Content-Security-Policy header.
findings.title: Content-Security-Policy
findings.what: There's no Content-Security-Policy, so if an attacker ever injects a script into a page (for example through a vulnerable plugin), the browser will run it.
findings.fix: Add a Content-Security-Policy header that lists the script, style, and image sources your site uses. Start in report-only mode, then enforce it.

findings.evidence: X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN
findings.title: Clickjacking protection
findings.what: Other websites can't secretly load your pages inside a frame.

findings.evidence: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
findings.title: X-Content-Type-Options
findings.what: Browsers are told not to guess file types, which blocks a class of file-upload tricks.

findings.evidence: No Referrer-Policy header (modern browsers fall back to a reasonable default, but older ones may leak full page addresses).
findings.title: Referrer-Policy
findings.what: Your site doesn't say how much of a page's address to share when visitors click a link to another site.

findings.evidence: No Permissions-Policy header.
findings.title: Permissions-Policy
findings.what: Your site doesn't limit which browser features (camera, microphone, location) pages and embedded content can ask for.
findings.fix: Add Permissions-Policy: camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=() (allow only what your site actually uses).

findings.evidence: harborbakery.example receives email via aspmx.l.google.com (Google Workspace).
findings.title: Email (MX) records
findings.what: This shows where email for your domain is delivered. It's background for the email checks.

findings.evidence: harborbakery.example: v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com ~all
findings.title: SPF record
findings.what: Your domain lists which servers are allowed to send email as you, which helps stop scammers sending fake emails from your address.

findings.evidence: No DMARC record found at _dmarc.harborbakery.example.
findings.title: DMARC policy
findings.what: There's no working DMARC policy, so email providers aren't told what to do with fake emails that use your domain (a common trick in invoice and payment scams).
findings.fix: Add a TXT record at _dmarc with v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:you@yourdomain to start, then move to p=quarantine or p=reject.

findings.evidence: DKIM not found on common selectors. We looked up 18 common selector names (google, selector1, selector2, default, k1, k2…) under harborbakery.example. Your email provider may use a different selector name, so this isn't proof that DKIM is turned off.
findings.title: DKIM signing
findings.what: We didn't find DKIM on the common selector names we know. Your provider may use a different name, so this isn't proof it's turned off.
findings.fix: Check your email provider's settings (Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, etc.) and confirm DKIM signing is turned on.

findings.evidence: Server: Apache/2.4.41 (Ubuntu); X-Powered-By: PHP/7.4.3; Page meta generator: WordPress 6.2.2
findings.title: Software version banners
findings.what: Your server advertises exact software versions, which tells attackers which known bugs to try.
findings.fix: Turn off version numbers in the Server and X-Powered-By headers (for example ServerTokens Prod in Apache, server_tokens off in nginx, expose_php = Off in PHP).

findings.evidence: Folder contents are publicly listed at: /wp-content/uploads/
findings.title: Directory listing
findings.what: Some folders on your site show a public list of every file inside, which can expose files you didn't mean to publish.
findings.fix: Have your developer or host turn off directory listing (for example Options -Indexes in Apache) and check what was exposed.

findings.evidence: Checked 10 commonly exposed sensitive files (like .env, .git, backups, phpinfo); none were publicly readable.
findings.title: Exposed sensitive files
findings.what: None of the commonly leaked sensitive files we checked are publicly readable.

findings.evidence: No /.well-known/security.txt file. It's optional: it tells security researchers how to report a problem to you.
findings.title: security.txt
findings.what: security.txt is an optional file that tells security researchers how to report problems. Nice to have, not required.

findings.evidence: 2 cookies set by the home page; all have the Secure flag.
findings.title: Cookie Secure flag
findings.what: Your cookies are only sent over encrypted connections.

findings.evidence: No HttpOnly flag on: wp_lang. None look like login or session cookies, and preference cookies often need to be readable by scripts.
findings.title: Cookie HttpOnly flag
findings.what: Some cookies don't have HttpOnly, but they don't look like login cookies, so that's usually fine.

findings.evidence: No SameSite attribute on: PHPSESSID.
findings.title: Cookie SameSite attribute
findings.what: Some cookies don't say when they can be sent from other sites. Modern browsers default to a safe setting, but older ones don't.
findings.fix: Add SameSite=Lax (or Strict) to those cookies.

scope: Passive check of the public home page, its HTTP headers, its certificate, public DNS records, and a short list of well-known file paths. No logins, form submissions, or attack traffic.
